solutions.check: 28 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: (see 26dn.) High Court division disposes of half of Tory fortune
Bone Clive and almost call out

indicators.note: almost a whole word means that word with its final letter missing
out suggests something put out of order, so the combined letters get rearranged

blocks.note: the name used as it stands

explanation.surface: Someone telling off a man called Clive, or nearly shouting his name.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Call out' reads as one phrasal verb; split it and 'out' is the signal for rearrangement while 'almost call' gives the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The collarbone, the long bone linking the shoulder blade to the breastbone, is its anatomical name.

clue.text: Celebrity arses in need of a lift

indicators.note: in a down entry, lifting a word means writing it from the bottom up

blocks.note: 'arses!' and 'rats!' are both British exclamations of annoyance

explanation.surface: A famous person whose backside could do with some cosmetic surgery.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes 'arses' a noun, bottoms needing a lift; it is really the exclamation, which RATS! matches.
explanation.definitionFit: A famous performer or public figure is commonly called a star, a standard synonym.

clue.text: A political upset in an election, by the the way, is touching

blocks.note: a seat taken from another party is a gain
ST, street, is a way; 'by' places it next in line

explanation.surface: A shock election result described as moving, with a chatty 'by the way' aside.
explanation.walkthrough: The printed clue doubles 'the'. 'By the way' looks like a set phrase, but 'by' only says ST comes beside the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Something leaning against a wall is in contact with it, so the preposition means in physical contact.

clue.text: (& 25ac.) Boris's 'cool tackle' could finish his career?

definitions.note: a verb phrase standing for a noun: something that could finish his career

blocks.note: Boris Johnson was the party leader, so 'Boris's' is the leader's
in football a tackle is an attempt to win the ball from an opponent, and the word for such an attempt also means a dare or test

explanation.surface: Boris Johnson's coolly executed tackle, perhaps on the rugby field, turning out to be career-ending.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs from 5 down into 25 across. 'Cool tackle' reads as one football term, but the words split; the possessive on Boris is part of the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A formal contest to unseat a party leader is the usual way a prime minister's time in office ends.

clue.text: Toss me a gin, poser!

indicators.note: tossing things throws them about, so the letters that follow land in new places

explanation.surface: A bar customer, perhaps a show-off, demanding that a gin be thrown over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poser' reads as a show-off posing for effect; here it is a puzzling question.
explanation.definitionFit: A poser is a baffling problem or puzzle, and an enigma is something mysterious and hard to work out.

clue.text: Spilt seed on time, penetrating mate, showing support

indicators.note: spilt things scatter, so the letters of the next word are scattered
one piece placed on another follows straight after it in a down entry
penetrating means going inside, so the first part goes into the word for mate

blocks.note: a pal is a mate, a friend

explanation.surface: An earthy scene of seed spilt in time with a partner, supposedly in a spirit of support.
explanation.walkthrough: The new order of the seed letters plus T for time go into PAL together, split after its P.
explanation.definitionFit: A pedestal is the base or plinth that holds up a statue or column, so it is literally a support.

clue.text: Hard drink smuggled into court house

indicators.note: smuggled goods are slipped inside, so the first pieces sit within the word for court

blocks.note: CT is the abbreviation for court

explanation.surface: Strong liquor being sneaked into a courthouse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hard drink' reads as one idea, spirits; it splits into H and ALE.
explanation.definitionFit: A chalet is a wooden Alpine-style dwelling or holiday cabin, a specific kind of house.

clue.text: Rene's broken into bloke's tax haven

indicators.note: a broken name falls apart, so the letters of the French name are rearranged
going into something means ending up inside it, so the rearranged name sits within the word for bloke

blocks.note: a guy is a bloke; the 's is simply 'is'
the five letters of Rene's, rearranged

explanation.surface: A Frenchman breaking into another man's offshore account, perhaps.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophes look possessive, but the S of Rene's is fodder, and bloke's just adds 'is' before the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The Channel Island is a Crown dependency with low taxes, famous for offshore finance, hence a tax haven.

clue.text: Pest gatecrashed study retreat – don't worry

indicators.note: retreating means going backwards, so the word for study runs in reverse
a gatecrasher gets inside uninvited, so the pest word ends up within the other piece

blocks.note: a den is a study, a private room for work

explanation.surface: A nuisance guest bursting in on a study retreat, and the host shrugging it off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Study retreat' looks like a residential course; it is DEN turned round.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are casual reassurances telling someone not to be concerned about something, so the phrases are interchangeable.

clue.text: European outs king as a nerd

indicators.note: to out someone is to put them out, so the king leaves the nationality word

blocks.note: R = rex, king; this letter is removed

explanation.surface: A European exposing a monarch as an awkward swot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outs' suggests exposing a secret; here it just means throws out.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe an obsessive, socially awkward enthusiast, usually of computers or science, so they are synonyms.

clue.text: Casually crush Lee, 'Labour powerhouse'

indicators.note: done casually means done carelessly, so the letters are thrown down in no set order

explanation.surface: A Labour Party heavyweight flattening a rival called Lee without effort.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital L makes 'Labour' look like the party; it is the twelve labours of the Greek hero.
explanation.definitionFit: The mythical strongman performed twelve great tasks known as labours, so he is a mighty figure of toil.

clue.text: Party with Conservative politician outside of a forced work environment

indicators.note: the politician word goes outside, wrapping round the little word after it

explanation.surface: A cross-party coalition that ends up feeling like a place of compulsory toil.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With' simply joins the pieces; 'outside of a' tells you the politician wraps round the single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A labour camp is a prison compound where inmates are made to do hard work, a place of compelled toil.

clue.text: Capri altogether too much as a tourist attraction

indicators.note: the two words hold too many letters, so the extra ones at each end are trimmed away

blocks.note: runs across the join of the two words

explanation.surface: A complaint that the island of Capri is simply overdone as a holiday spot.
explanation.walkthrough: Capri is the obvious attraction, but it is only the container; the answer is in Venice.
explanation.definitionFit: The Rialto Bridge over the Grand Canal in Venice is one of the city's best-known sights for visitors.

clue.text: Access to penis? Heartless lad passes quickly

indicators.note: without a heart means the middle letter of the word for lad goes

blocks.note: trouser flies, the zipped opening at the front
BOY with its central O removed

explanation.surface: A cheeky question about trouser access, then a youth rushing past.
explanation.walkthrough: Flies are the fly opening on trousers, a British plural; 'heartless lad' is BOY losing its middle.
explanation.definitionFit: When time or scenery flies by it goes past at speed, so the phrasal verb means moves past rapidly.

clue.text: Inclined to squeeze tip of todger, being a student?

definitions.note: a participle phrase for a participle

indicators.note: a tip can be either end; here it is the final letter of the rude word
to squeeze something is to hold it tight inside, so the word for inclined grips the letter

blocks.note: todger is British slang for penis

explanation.surface: Someone inclined to grab a penis, with a mock-innocent question about studying.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tip' tempts you to take the T at the start of todger; the tip needed is the other end.
explanation.definitionFit: A student is someone in the process of acquiring knowledge, so being one means studying and gaining skills.

clue.text: Balls caught in turning wheel – be persuasive

indicators.note: turning shifts the letters of wheel round into a new order
something caught in a thing is trapped inside it, so the politician sits within the other letters

blocks.note: Ed Balls, the Labour politician and former shadow chancellor

explanation.surface: A ball game image of balls trapped in a wheel, with a plea to be persuasive.
explanation.walkthrough: Balls seem to be spheres or testicles; Private Eye readers know Ed Balls, so 'Balls' gives ED.
explanation.definitionFit: To wheedle is to coax someone with flattery and sweet talk, which is a way of persuading them.

clue.text: 'New' Brown embraced with unbridled glee? Get knotted!

definitions.note: an intransitive phrase for a transitive verb

indicators.note: an unbridled horse runs wild, so the letters of glee run loose
to be embraced is to be held inside, so the first pieces sit within the jumbled word

explanation.surface: Gordon Brown's New Labour, gleefully embraced, told to push off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get knotted!' is British slang for 'go away'; taken literally it means become tangled. 'New' Brown reads as Gordon Brown's New Labour.
explanation.definitionFit: To entangle is to twist into a tangle, so it describes something ending up in knots.

clue.text: Penis initially tending to be bendy

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the opening letter of the word before it counts

blocks.note: liable to = tending to, inclined to

explanation.surface: A rude observation that a penis often has a bend in it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tending to' looks like part of the surface grammar; 'liable to' means inclined to, so 'tending' supplies LIABLE.
explanation.definitionFit: Something pliable is flexible and easily bent without breaking, so the adjectives are synonyms.

clue.text: Dodgy as a Sun's tourist destination

indicators.note: something dodgy is not quite right, so the letters after it are out of order

blocks.note: six letters of fodder; 's then joins to the definition

explanation.surface: A jibe that a travel spot is as dodgy as a Sun newspaper holiday offer.
explanation.walkthrough: The Sun is a British tabloid, which is what makes the surface sneer; its letters are simply fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Nassau, the capital of the Bahamas, is a popular Caribbean resort and cruise port for holidaymakers.

clue.text: see 26dn.
Mouthy thing – cheek! – wants poke

blocks.note: to stick is to poke or jab

explanation.surface: A lippy person, all cheek, spoiling for a jab.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mouthy' looks like cheeky talk, which suits 'cheek'; the definition means a thing for the mouth.
explanation.definitionFit: Lipstick is a cosmetic applied to the lips, so it is literally an item that belongs on the mouth.

clue.text: Arse-like revolutionary figure misplaced key

definitions.note: a jokey sense: like cheeks, the buttocks

indicators.note: misplaced letters are put in the wrong positions, so the word for key is rearranged

explanation.surface: A rebel icon, shaped like a backside, who has lost his key.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a joke: cheeks are buttocks, so arse-like is cheeky, though the usual meaning is impudent.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheeks is slang for buttocks, so the adjective is punningly read as resembling a bottom.

clue.text: One presidential candidate who failed, just like an arse

blocks.note: Al Gore lost the 2000 US election

explanation.surface: A losing US candidate insulted as a complete arse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Arse' is British for backside, and 'like an arse' is taken literally.
explanation.definitionFit: Anal is the adjective for the anus, so it describes things relating to the backside.

clue.text: see 5dn.
(&1dn./21dn.) Enchant with a colossal bust – an opportunity that can't be missed

definitions.text: an opportunity that can't be missed

indicators.note: something bust is broken, so the letters of the words before it are smashed and reassembled

blocks.note: taken letter for letter as fodder
the rest of the fodder; 'with' just joins the two pieces

explanation.surface: A spell cast using a gigantic bust, promoted as a chance nobody should pass up.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is spread over 26, 1 and 21 down. 1 down also carries its own clue: CHANCERY (a High Court division) drops RY, half of TORY, to leave CHANCE, fortune.
explanation.definitionFit: A last-chance saloon is an idiom for a final opportunity to put things right before failure becomes certain.

clue.text: Playing nicely with a lady's top, but not stiff

blocks.note: a player playing well is in form

explanation.surface: Someone fondling a woman's top nicely, with a smutty undertone about stiffness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lady's top' looks like a blouse; it is only her first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Relaxed and casual behaviour is the opposite of formal stiffness, so informal means unstarchy.

clue.text: In fairness, Al (Ukip) is a dog

indicators.note: the answer sits in the words that follow, spanning their joins

blocks.note: runs from the end of fairness through Al into Ukip

explanation.surface: A fair-minded verdict that a UKIP politician called Al is a dog.
explanation.walkthrough: UKIP is a British anti-EU party; the brackets and comma are punctuation the solver ignores, so the answer runs straight through them.
explanation.definitionFit: The saluki is a slender Middle Eastern sighthound breed, so it is one kind of dog.
